title: June 2019 (Shift 1)
subtitle: Verified Answer Key (100/100 Qs) + Crisp Simple-English Explanations

items.title: Q1 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit II: Poetry · Thomas Hardy
items.stem: Which of the following poems by Thomas Hardy was originally titled By the Century's Deathbed?
items.explanation: Hardy wrote 'The Darkling Thrush' on 31 December 1900. It first appeared under the title 'By the Century's Deathbed'.

items.title: Q2 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which of the following descriptions fits the unit of verse, Dactyl?
options: One stressed syllable followed by three unstressed syllables
One stressed syllable followed by two unstressed syllables
Two stressed syllables followed by one unstressed syllable
Two stressed syllables followed by two unstressed syllables
items.explanation: A dactyl is a metrical foot of one stressed syllable followed by two unstressed ones (/ u u), as in 'TEN-der-ly'.

items.title: Q3 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods · Umberto Eco
items.stem: Who wrote a guide called How to Write a Doctoral Thesis : The Humanistic Subjects, considered equal in standard to the American MLS Handbook or The Chicago Manual of Style?
items.explanation: Umberto Eco wrote 'How to Write a Thesis' (originally in Italian, 1977), a famous practical guide for humanities students.

items.title: Q4 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Who of the following are being talked about in the following lines?
"... you seem to understand me,
By each at once her choppy finger laying
Upon her skinny lips : you should be women,
And yet your beards forbid me to interpret
That you are so."
items.explanation: Banquo speaks these lines in Macbeth (Act 1, Scene 3). He sees the Weird Sisters, who look like women but have beards.

items.title: Q5 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy · Ferdinand de Saussure
items.stem: What is the meaning of 'langue' in Saussurean linguistics?
options: The dialectic between thought and speech
items.explanation: For Saussure, 'langue' is the shared system of signs and differences behind speech. 'Parole' is the individual speech act.

items.title: Q6 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Rohinton Mistry
items.stem: Who is the author of the short story, The Ghost of Firozsha Baag?
items.explanation: 'The Ghost of Firozsha Baag' is a story in Rohinton Mistry's collection 'Tales from Firozsha Baag' (1987).

items.title: Q7 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Lao Tzu
items.stem:
All in the world know the beauty of the beautiful, and in doing this they have (the idea of) what ugliness is; they all know the skill of the skillful, and in doing this they have (the idea of) what the want of the skill is.
So it is that existence and non-existence gave birth to (the idea of) the other; that difficulty and ease produce (the idea of) the other; that the length and shortness fashion out the one figure of the other; that (the idea of) height and lowness arise from the contrast of one with the other; that the musical notes and tones become harmonious through the relation of one with another; and that being before and behind give the idea of one following another.

Which one of the following is the correct meaning of the ominous little phrase 'the idea of' in the first sentence of the passage?
items.explanation: The passage (from the Tao Te Ching) says we know beauty only by also having a notion of ugliness. 'The idea of' therefore points to a prior knowledge of the opposite.

items.title: Q8 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Classical Greece (Attic Age) · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: From which Greek word does the term 'comedy' derive and what does it mean?
items.explanation: 'Comedy' comes from Greek 'komoidia', from 'komos' (revel, festive procession) and 'oide' (song), so it means a revel-song.

items.title: Q9 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Ziauddin Sardar
items.stem:
What is the meaning of Ziauddin Sardar's statement?
"Cultural studies started as a dissenting intellectual tradition outside academia, dedicated to exposing power in all its cultural forms. But it has now become a discipline and a part of the academic establishment and its power structure."
items.explanation: Sardar says a once-rebellious outsider tradition has become a formal academic discipline. That process is called institutionalisation.

items.title: Q10 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · George Orwell
items.stem: Which of the following works is reviewed in George Orwell's essay, Inside the Whale?
items.explanation: Orwell's 'Inside the Whale' (1940) is a long review-essay on Henry Miller's novel 'Tropic of Cancer'.

items.title: Q11 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · T. S. Eliot, Virgil
items.stem: Why did T. S. Eliot assert that Virgil, not Homer, is the poet of Europe?
options: There are some initial moral concerns in Virgil
Virgil belongs to the Roman period
Homer was a pagan who was a renegade
Virgil wrote in Latin while Homer wrote in Greek
items.explanation: In 'What is a Classic?' Eliot ties Virgil to Rome and its imperial destiny, which shaped Europe's idea of civilisation.

items.title: Q12 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · William Wordsworth
items.stem: Which edition of the Lyrical Ballads was the first one to have the Preface by Wordsworth?
items.explanation: The Preface first appeared in the second edition of 'Lyrical Ballads' in 1800. It was expanded in 1802.

items.title: Q13 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · T. S. Eliot
items.stem: In Eliot's Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock who among the following painters is the subject of conversation among the perambulating women?
items.explanation: The refrain 'In the room the women come and go / Talking of Michelangelo' refers to Michelangelo.

items.title: Q14 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: Which type of textual copy is concerned with an assessment of the physical details of the books and their exact relationship to the condition in which the book was planned to appear at the time of its initial publication?
items.explanation: In bibliography an 'ideal copy' is the book as the publisher intended it to appear. Real copies are compared against it.

items.title: Q15 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Jane Austen
items.stem: Which one of the following novels of Jane Austen was abandoned unfinished?
items.explanation: Austen left 'The Watsons' unfinished (about 1805). The other three were completed and published.

items.title: Q16 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · J. G. Farrell
items.stem: Which novel by J. G. Farrell describes the experiences of a polio victim?
items.explanation: 'The Lung' (1965) is Farrell's novel based on his own bout of polio, written while he was recovering.

items.title: Q17 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Who speaks the following lines and to whom?
"O, look upon me, sir,
And hold your hands in benediction o'er me.
No, sir, you must not kneel."
items.explanation: In King Lear Act 4 Scene 7, Cordelia says this to the waking Lear when he tries to kneel to her.

items.title: Q18 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Francis Bacon
items.stem: "He that is not with us is against us. He that is not against us is with us." Who said this?
items.explanation: Bacon quotes the two Biblical sayings in his essay 'Of Unity in Religion' to discuss religious factions.

items.title: Q19 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem:
Match the character with the novel :
Character / Novel
(a) Kate / (i) Great Expectations
(b) Florence / (ii) Nicholas Nickleby
(c) Miss Havisham / (iii) David Copperfield
(d) Agnes / (iv) Dombey and Son
Choose the correct option from those given below :
items.explanation: Kate is in Nicholas Nickleby, Florence in Dombey and Son, Miss Havisham in Great Expectations and Agnes in David Copperfield.

items.title: Q20 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India · Charles Wood
items.stem:
Which of the following two points were emphasised by 'Wood's Despatch of 1854'?
(a) Teaching of the English language along with the study of vernacular language
(b) Compulsory inclusion of Christianity in the curriculum
(c) The gradual withdrawal of government patronage from Indian languages
(d) The importance of female education
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: Wood's Despatch urged English teaching alongside vernaculars and promoted female education. It did not impose Christianity or withdraw support from Indian languages.

items.title: Q21 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Classical Greece (Attic Age) · Unit I: Drama · Sophocles
items.stem: What is the Priest's entreaty to Oedipus in the opening scene of Oedipus Rex?
options: To liberate Thebes from the domination of the Sphinx
To rid Thebes of the plague that afflicts its people
To afford the Thebans the luxury of newer forms of worship
To send Creon to seek advice from the oracle of Delphi
items.explanation: The Priest begs Oedipus, who once saved the city from the Sphinx, to save Thebes again from the plague.

items.title: Q22 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit I: Drama · T. S. Eliot
items.stem:
"The last temptation is the greatest treason
To do the right deed for the wrong reason."
(T. S. Eliot, Murder in the Cathedral)
Why is the 'temptation', 'treason' for the speaker of the lines?
items.explanation: Becket fears seeking martyrdom for his own glory. A good act done for a selfish reason betrays the cause.

items.title: Q23 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Herman Melville, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Edgar Allan Poe, Henry James
items.stem: Which one of the following groups of novelists has, in the given order, Captain Ahab, Hester Prynne, Roderick Usher and Daisy Miller as characters in their novels?
options: Henry James, Edgar A. Poe, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Herman Melville
Herman Melville, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Edgar A. Poe, Henry James
Edgar A. Poe, Henry James, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Herman Melville
Nathaniel Hawthorne, Edgar A. Poe, Henry James, Herman Melville
items.explanation: Ahab is Melville's, Hester Prynne is Hawthorne's, Roderick Usher is Poe's and Daisy Miller is James's.

items.title: Q24 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit I: Drama
items.stem:
Match each of the following concepts/objects with the corresponding description :
(a) Farce / (i) Articles and objects used on the stage
(b) Props / (ii) Drama written to be read rather than acted
(c) Music hall / (iii) Characterized by broad humour, wild antics, slapsticks etc.
(d) Closet drama / (iv) Variety entertainment of songs, comic turns that flourished in England through the late 19th Century
Choose the correct option from those given below :
items.explanation: Farce is broad slapstick comedy, props are stage objects, music hall is variety entertainment and closet drama is meant for reading.

items.title: Q25 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
Which of the following combinations correctly defines the phonological system of Indian English in relation to Standard English?
(a) Absence of aspirated consonants
(b) Simplified vowel system
(c) Similar international pattern
(d) Presence of voiced aspirated consonants
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: Indian English has a simpler vowel system than Standard English and keeps voiced aspirates (like bh, dh) from Indian languages.

items.title: Q26 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · John Lyly
items.stem: What is 'euphuism'?
options: Eulogical and adulatory style of writing
Discursive and hortatory style of writing
Pompous and affected style of writing
Exalted and grand style of writing
items.explanation: Euphuism is an elaborate, affected prose style named after John Lyly's 'Euphues' (1578).

items.title: Q27 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Which one of the following paired terms is correct in its explication?
items.explanation: Phonology studies sound systems. Semiology is the study of signs, etymology is the origin of words and morphology is word structure.

items.title: Q28 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · T. S. Eliot, William Shakespeare
items.stem: Which of the following statements best describes T. S. Eliot's assertion that Shakespeare's Hamlet is an 'artistic failure'?
options: Hamlet's emotion is not adequately objectified
Hamlet's feelings far outweigh the release of his emotions
Hamlet's obsession should have been within representational limits
Hamlet's indecisiveness slows the steady progress of action
items.explanation: In 'Hamlet and His Problems' Eliot says there is no 'objective correlative' for Hamlet's emotion, so it exceeds the facts presented.

items.title: Q29 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Michel Foucault
items.stem: Who among the following explored the shifting and contested power-relations, knowledge and the human body?
items.explanation: Foucault studied how power, knowledge and the body are linked and contested, in works like 'Discipline and Punish'.

items.title: Q30 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Roland Barthes, Terry Eagleton, M. H. Abrams, Raymond Williams
items.stem:
Match the works with authors :
Works / Authors
(a) Image-Music-Text / (i) M. H. Abrams
(b) Why Marx was Right / (ii) Raymond Williams
(c) The Mirror and the Lamp / (iii) Roland Barthes
(d) Culture and Society / (iv) Terry Eagleton
Choose the correct option from those given below :
items.explanation: Barthes wrote Image-Music-Text, Eagleton wrote Why Marx was Right, Abrams wrote The Mirror and the Lamp and Williams wrote Culture and Society.

items.title: Q31 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Age of Johnson, Sensibility & Pre-Romantic Transition · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Samuel Johnson, William Shakespeare
items.stem:
From among the following, identify the two correct statements in Johnson's criticism of Shakespeare :
(a) His Athenians are not sufficiently Greek and his kings not completely royal.
(b) He sacrifices virtue to convenience and is more careful to please than to instruct.
(c) He adheres to strict chronology and gives to one age or nation only its own customs and opinions.
(d) He sacrifices reason, property and truth to pursue even a poor and barren quibble.
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: In his Preface Johnson faults Shakespeare for weak morality and for chasing quibbles. He also says Shakespeare mixes customs of different ages, so (a) and (c) are wrong.

items.title: Q32 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · John Keats
items.stem: Who among the following is celebrated in John Keats's Lines on the Mermaid Tavern?
items.explanation: The poem imagines Robin Hood and Maid Marian feasting on venison pies, comparing that feast to the Mermaid Tavern's poets.

items.title: Q33 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Roland Barthes
items.stem: Who among the following analysed the naturalisation of connotative meanings into myths?
items.explanation: In 'Mythologies' Barthes shows how connotations are made to look natural and become myths.

items.title: Q34 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit II: Poetry · Ezra Pound
items.stem:
Read the following lines :
IN A STATION OF THE METRO
The apparition of these faces in the crowd :
Petals on a wet, black bough.
Which of the following poetic programmes is illustrated by the above lines?
items.explanation: Pound's two-line poem is a classic Imagist work: a sharp, compressed image with no comment.

items.title: Q35 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · W. Somerset Maugham
items.stem: Identify the author in whose works the character Ashenden appears many times :
items.explanation: Ashenden is Maugham's spy-agent hero in 'Ashenden: or The British Agent' and other stories.

items.title: Q36 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy · Noam Chomsky
items.stem: In which of the following paired terms, the relationship between the active and passive forms of a sentence can be best established?
items.explanation: In Chomsky's grammar, active and passive sentences share one deep structure but have different surface structures.

items.title: Q37 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Michel Foucault
items.stem:
By which two of the following processes, according to Michel Foucault, does power operate?
(a) By right rather than technique
(b) By normalization rather than law
(c) By control rather than punishment
(d) By repression rather than agreement
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: Foucault argues modern power works through normalization and control, not through law and punishment alone.

items.title: Q38 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · F. R. Leavis
items.stem: "The great English novelists are Jane Austen, George Eliot, Henry James and Joseph Conrad." Which one of the following critical texts begins with the above assertion?
options: F. R. Leavis, The Great Tradition
Ian Watt, Rise of the Novel
items.explanation: This is the opening sentence of F. R. Leavis's 'The Great Tradition' (1948).

items.title: Q39 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem:
Match the following journals with their distinguishing aims and methods of scholarship :
(a) Obsidian / (i) Literature, history and the philosophy of history
(b) Clio / (ii) Literature and arts in the African diaspora
(c) Interventions / (iii) Feminist writing
(d) Signs / (iv) Postcolonial writing
Choose the correct option from those given below :
items.explanation: Obsidian covers African diaspora arts, Clio covers literature and history, Interventions is postcolonial and Signs is feminist.

items.title: Q40 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · E. D. Hirsch, Martin Heidegger
items.stem:
Identify the two names from the following who are associated with Hermeneutics :
(a) Edmund Husserl
(b) E. D. Hirsch
(c) Martin Heidegger
(d) Stephen Greenblatt
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: Hirsch ('Validity in Interpretation') and Heidegger are central to hermeneutics. Husserl is a phenomenologist and Greenblatt a New Historicist.

items.title: Q41 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Augustan Age (Age of Pope & Swift) · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Laurence Sterne, Henry Fielding, Frances Burney, Daniel Defoe
items.stem:
Match the Novelist with the Publisher :
(a) Laurence Sterne / (i) Thomas Lowndes
(b) Henry Fielding / (ii) Andrew Millar
(c) Frances Burney / (iii) William Taylor
(d) Daniel Defoe / (iv) Robert Dodsley
Choose the correct option from those given below :
items.explanation: Dodsley published Sterne, Millar published Fielding, Lowndes published Burney's Evelina and Taylor published Robinson Crusoe.

items.title: Q42 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Philip Sidney, P. B. Shelley
items.stem:
Which two writers have written essays on the defence of poetry?
(a) Sir Philip Sidney
(b) P.B. Shelley
(c) Dr. Mathew Arnold
(d) T.S. Eliot
Choose the correct option :
items.explanation: Sidney wrote 'An Apology for Poetry' and Shelley wrote 'A Defence of Poetry'.

items.title: Q43 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit I: Drama
items.stem: Which of the following is the accurate description of 'dramatic irony'?
options: A character's knowledge or expectation is contradicted by what the audience knows, or by the outcome of events
An audience knows or expects something to happen but the events on stage turn out to be different
Ironic events and expectations of actual actions and results converge in drama and the audience feels rewarded
A dramatist's irony reinforces his actors' performance, thereby fulfilling audience expectations
items.explanation: In dramatic irony the audience knows more than a character does, so the character's words or hopes are contradicted.

items.title: Q44 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem:
Given below are two statements—one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R) :
Assertion (A) : Instances of beliefs triggering action are present in social life and may give rise to problems in determining 'causality'.
Reason (R) : Beliefs may not be accompanied by or give rise to logically appropriate actions, and actions may occur which are consistent with motivations and intentions, but they often, if not usually, also have unanticipated outcomes.
In the light of the above two statements choose the correct option :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
items.explanation: Both statements are true. Beliefs and actions do not link neatly and have unexpected results, which is why causality is hard to fix.

items.title: Q45 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem:
Who says the following lines and to whom?
"If it be aught toward the general good,
Set honor in one eye and death i' th' other,
And I will look on both indifferently."
items.explanation: Brutus says this to Cassius in Julius Caesar (Act 1, Scene 2), showing he values the public good above honour or death.

items.title: Q46 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem: Which one of the following correctly describes the meaning of Macbeth's words '... life is but a walking shadow'?
options: Life is just devoid of light
Life is just devoid of substance
Life is just devoid of spirit
Life is just devoid of stability
items.explanation: A shadow has no substance, so Macbeth calls life empty and without real meaning.

items.title: Q47 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · William Hazlitt, William Wordsworth
items.stem: Which of the following poets does William Hazlitt call 'Don Quixote-like' in his essay, My First Acquaintance with Poets?
items.explanation: Hazlitt describes Wordsworth's tall, gaunt figure as 'something of a Don Quixote-like appearance'.

items.title: Q48 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Late Victorian, Aestheticism & Fin-de-Siecle · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Oscar Wilde
items.stem: For which one of the following reasons, in Oscar Wilde's novel, The Picture of Dorian Gray, Gray breaks down when he sees his finished portrait?
options: Overwhelmed by the beauty of the portrait
Overjoyed by the feeling that his beauty will be known to all
Distraught by the fact that his beauty will fade while the portrait stays beautiful
Distraught by the badly drawn portrait
items.explanation: Dorian realises he will grow old while the portrait stays young, and he wishes it were the other way round.

items.title: Q49 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Edward Said, Terry Eagleton, Francis Mulhern, K. M. Newton
items.stem:
Match the critics and their works :
Critics / Works
(a) Edward Said / (i) The Illusions of Postmodernism
(b) Terry Eagleton / (ii) Contemporary Marxist Criticism
(c) Francis Mulhern / (iii) Theory into Practice
(d) K. M. Newton / (iv) Culture and Imperialism
Choose the correct option from those given below :
items.explanation: Said wrote Culture and Imperialism, Eagleton wrote The Illusions of Postmodernism, Mulhern wrote Contemporary Marxist Criticism and Newton wrote Theory into Practice.

items.title: Q50 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · J. Hillis Miller, Marcel Mauss
items.stem: Which of the following sociologists' ideas on the practice of receiving and giving gifts are used by J. Hillis Miller to reinforce her arguments in the essay, Critic as Host?
items.explanation: Miller draws on Marcel Mauss's 'The Gift' to discuss host, guest and the exchange of gifts in criticism.

items.title: Q51 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early Tudor & Humanist Reformation · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas More
items.stem: Which of the following books is written by an Englishman in universal Latin, is further added to by the Flemish Peter Giles, is revised by the Dutch Erasmus, is printed at Louvain in 1516, later at Paris, still later at Basle, where it was illustrated by two woodcuts from the hand of the German Holbein?
items.explanation: Thomas More wrote 'Utopia' in Latin (1516). Giles, Erasmus and Holbein were all linked with its early editions.

items.title: Q52 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem:
The Sadler Commission Report (1917-1919) was critical of the quality of students graduating from the university and had very perceptive remarks on English and the use of mother tongue in Indian education.
What was this Commission appointed for?
options: To examine the functioning of the Directorate of Public Instruction in Delhi
To study the problems of Calcutta University
To investigate and recommend teaching methods of languages generally
To evolve a three-language formula for the Indian schools
items.explanation: The Calcutta University Commission (1917-19) under Michael Sadler studied the problems of Calcutta University.

items.title: Q53 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Sandra Gilbert and Susan Gubar, Frantz Fanon, Stephen Greenblatt, Stanley Fish
items.stem:
Match the books with the writers :
(a) The Madwoman in the Attic / (i) Frantz Fanon
(b) The Wretched of the Earth / (ii) Stephen Greenblatt
(c) Shakespearean Negotiations / (iii) Stanley Fish
(d) Is There a Text in This Class? / (iv) Sandra M. Gilbert and Susan Gubar
Choose the correct option from those given below :
items.explanation: The Madwoman in the Attic is by Gilbert and Gubar, The Wretched of the Earth by Fanon, Shakespearean Negotiations by Greenblatt and Is There a Text in This Class? by Fish.

items.title: Q54 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy · Daniel Jones
items.stem: Who among the following established and popularised the concept of 'Cardinal Vowels'?
items.explanation: The phonetician Daniel Jones devised the Cardinal Vowel system as reference points for describing vowel sounds.

items.title: Q55 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Stephen Greenblatt
items.stem: Which writer applied the term 'cultural poetics' to his own critical contribution to make literature and arts as part of social practice?
items.explanation: Greenblatt preferred 'cultural poetics' to 'New Historicism' for his method of reading literature within social practice.

items.title: Q56 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: Which one of the following is the right definition of 'peer review'?
options: A post-publication process in which the work is submitted to a panel of reviewers for ascertaining quality
A pre-publication process in which work submitted for publication is evaluated for quality by experts in the field
A pre-publication process in which work submitted for publication is accompanied by recommendation of other experts in the field
A post-publication process in which the work is submitted for a professional review
items.explanation: Peer review happens before publication: independent experts assess the quality of a submitted work.

items.title: Q57 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Raymond Williams
items.stem: What, according to Raymond Williams, is the right description of the term 'Cultural Materialism'?
options: The cultural effect that religion has in social life
The political effect that matter has in social lives
The material effect that culture has in wider social life
The effect of social life in cultural situations of uncertainty
items.explanation: Williams treats culture as a material force. Cultural materialism studies the material effect culture has on social life.

items.title: Q58 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · P. B. Shelley, Plato
items.stem: Which one of the following of Plato's beliefs/acts was Shelley countering by saying that 'poets are the unacknowledged legislators of mankind'?
options: Banishment of poets from the republic
Distrust of value of poetry for mankind
Description of poets as mad men
items.explanation: Plato banished poets from his ideal Republic. Shelley answers in 'A Defence of Poetry' that poets are the true lawgivers of humanity.

items.title: Q59 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India · Charles Grant
items.stem: Which of the following propositions refers to the recommendations of Charles Grant?
options: The introduction of English as the medium of instruction in an Indian system of education that included literature, art and craft
The introduction of English as the medium of instruction from lower levels in a few states as an experiment
The introduction of English as the medium of instruction in a Western system of education that included literature, natural sciences and mechanical inventions
The introduction of English as the medium of instruction in regional medium institutions that included only literature
items.explanation: Grant argued for teaching English and a Western curriculum of literature, science and useful arts to Indians.

items.title: Q60 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Samuel Taylor Coleridge
items.stem: "To see him act is like reading Shakespeare by flashes of lighting." About which Shakespearean actor Coleridge wrote the above line?
items.explanation: Coleridge said this of Edmund Kean, whose acting was brilliant in sudden flashes.

items.title: Q61 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Jacques Lacan
items.stem: Identify the stage that falls between the imaginary and symbolic stages according to Jacques Lacan :
items.explanation: The only sensible option is 'intermediate stage' as a stage lying between the imaginary and the symbolic.

items.title: Q62 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods · W. W. Greg
items.stem: Who is the author of the essay, The Rationale of the Copy-Text?
items.explanation: W. W. Greg published 'The Rationale of Copy-Text' in 1950. It is a foundation of modern textual editing.

items.title: Q63 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Thomas Carlyle
items.stem: Which among the following clusters matches the prose style that came to be known as 'Carlylese'?
options: Capital letters, exclamation marks, phrases in German
Question marks, long sentences, phrases in French
Frequent ellipses, Latin sayings, comic non-sequitors
Biblical phrases, capital letters, missing letters
items.explanation: Carlyle's odd prose used capitals, exclamations and German-flavoured phrases.

items.title: Q64 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem: Which of the following aptly names the language resulting from the contact of two mutually unintelligible language systems?
items.explanation: A pidgin is a simple contact language that develops between groups with no common language. A creole is a pidgin that becomes a native language.

items.title: Q65 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) · Unit II: Poetry · Layamon, William Langland, William Dunbar
items.stem: Which one of the following arrangements of poets is in the correct chronological order?
items.explanation: Layamon wrote around 1200, Langland in the late 1300s and Dunbar around 1500.

items.title: Q66 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · F. J. Turner, Gertrude Stein, Homi Bhabha, Raymond Williams
items.stem:
Match the following items/ideas with the writers who first used/popularized them :
(a) The Frontier Thesis / (i) Raymond Williams
(b) The Lost Generation / (ii) Homi Bhabha
(c) Third Space / (iii) F. J. Turner
(d) Structure of Feeling / (iv) Gertrude Stein
Choose the correct option from those given below :
items.explanation: Turner proposed the Frontier Thesis, Stein popularised 'Lost Generation', Bhabha the 'Third Space' and Williams the 'Structure of Feeling'.

items.title: Q67 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Wordsworth
items.explanation: In 'The Thorn' the narrator measures a small mound beside the thorn tree, which is the grave of Martha Ray's infant.

items.title: Q68 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early Tudor & Humanist Reformation · Unit II: Poetry · John Skelton
items.stem:
What is the name of the poetic style characterized by short staccato rhymed lines, as shown below?
What can it avayle
To dryve forth a snayle,
Or to make a sayle
Of a herynges tayle?
items.explanation: Short, rapid, rhyming lines are the hallmark of John Skelton's verse, called Skeltonics.

items.title: Q69 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which of the following statements is true in terms of distribution of metrical feet?
options: Anapaestic is to Dactylic as Trochaic is to Iambic
Trochaic is to Anapaestic as Dactylic is to Iambic
Iambic is to Trochaic as Anapaestic is to Dactylic
Dactylic is to Trochaic as Iambic is to Anapaestic
items.explanation: The iamb (u /) is the reverse of the trochee (/ u), and the anapaest (u u /) is the reverse of the dactyl (/ u u).

items.title: Q70 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy · Ferdinand de Saussure, Noam Chomsky
items.stem: What term used by Ferdinand de Saussure corresponds to Noam Chomsky's term 'performance'?
items.explanation: Saussure's 'parole' (actual speech) matches Chomsky's 'performance', while 'langue' matches 'competence'.

items.title: Q71 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-Independence Indian English, Postcolonial & Global Anglophone Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Anita Desai
items.stem: In which of Anita Desai's novels does an insane wife kill her husband?
items.explanation: In 'Cry, the Peacock' Maya, haunted by a prophecy, goes mad and pushes her husband Gautama off the roof.

items.title: Q72 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Iris Murdoch
items.stem: Which of the following novels by Iris Murdoch tells the story of an ageing theatre celebrity who withdraws into a life of seclusion and writes a diary/journal/novel?
items.explanation: In 'The Sea, the Sea' (1978) Charles Arrowby, a retired theatre director, writes his memoir by the sea.

items.title: Q73 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Which of the following correctly describes 'black humour' as a morbid and provocative treatment of
items.explanation: Black humour treats grim subjects such as death and disease in a comic, provocative way.

items.title: Q74 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Jacobean Period · Unit I: Drama · William Shakespeare
items.stem: In which play, other than Julius Caesar, has Shakespeare depicted the Romans better than the Roman writers themselves have done?
items.explanation: Among the options, only Coriolanus is a Roman play, and it is praised for its Roman portrait.

items.title: Q75 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Antonio Gramsci
items.stem: What was Gramsci's term for cultural consensus supporting capitalism?
items.explanation: Gramsci's 'hegemony' means the rule of a class through consent, shaped by culture, rather than by force alone.

items.title: Q76 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Early & Mid-Victorian Britain · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem: Considering the story of the novel, what does the title Dombey and Son stand for?
options: It suggests the choice between a son and a daughter
It suggests the commercial aspect of life
It suggests the opposition between a father and a son
It suggests the importance of a dynasty
items.explanation: Mr Dombey wants a son to carry on his firm and name. The title reflects his obsession with dynasty.

items.title: Q77 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods
items.stem: While looking for publication details of a book, a researcher may consult the book's copyright page, which may appear
options: usually the reverse of the title page
invariably the reverse of the title page
items.explanation: The copyright page is usually printed on the back of the title page, though not always.

items.title: Q78 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: High Modernism, WWI Trench Poets & The 1930s Auden Generation · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · T. S. Eliot
items.stem:
Which one of the following is the source of the passage given below?
"I have observed with growing anxiety the career of this word culture during the past six or seven years. We may find it natural, and significant, that during a period of unparalleled destructiveness, this word should come to have an important role..."
options: F.R. Leavis, Mass Civilization and Minority Culture
T.S. Eliot, Notes Towards the Definition of Culture
Stuart Hall, Cultural Representations and Signifying Practices
items.explanation: This is from the opening of T. S. Eliot's 'Notes towards the Definition of Culture' (1948).

items.title: Q79 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel Modernist Tracks: American Modernism, Harlem Renaissance & Indian Gandhian Era · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story
items.stem: What does 'Harlem Renaissance' refer to?
options: A scientific and rational ethos, including freedom from superstition, in 18th century Europe
The flourishing of African American literature in the 1920s and 1930s
A church system, overseen by a governing hierarchy of four courts, championed by the English Puritans
The revelation of Christ to the Gentiles in the persons of the Magi
items.explanation: The Harlem Renaissance was the cultural and literary flowering of African American writers and artists in the 1920s and 1930s.

items.title: Q80 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · William Golding
items.stem: Who is referred to as 'beast' in the quote 'Kill the beast! Cut his throat! Spill his blood' in William Golding's Lord of the Flies?
items.explanation: The boys, in a frenzied dance, mistake Simon for the beast and kill him.

items.title: Q81 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit I: Drama · Samuel Beckett
items.stem: Which of the following plays is characterized by the exclusivity of a single character talking to himself?
items.explanation: Beckett's 'Krapp's Last Tape' has one character, Krapp, who listens to and talks to his old recordings.

items.title: Q82 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language & ELT Pedagogy
items.stem:
Given below are two statements—one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R) :
Assertion (A) : The dialects of English that have resulted from the regional separation of English-speaking communities have not acquired the status of languages.
Reason (R) : The Germanic dialects that are now Dutch, English, German, Swedish etc., have become distinct owing to geographical dispersion.
In the light of the above two statements choose the correct option :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
items.explanation: Both statements are true, but the Germanic dispersion is a different case. It does not explain why English dialects stay dialects.

items.title: Q83 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: The Age of Chaucer (Ricardian 14th Century) · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: The medieval English university organized its studies based on the seven liberal arts. Three of these, the trivium, referred to the study of
items.explanation: The trivium was grammar, logic and rhetoric. The quadrivium was arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy.

items.title: Q84 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Raymond Williams
items.stem: "Culture is ordinary : that is the first fact." Which one of the following is the source of this statement?
items.explanation: 'Culture is Ordinary' is an essay by Raymond Williams, collected in 'Resources of Hope' (1989).

items.title: Q85 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Parallel 19th-C Tracks: American Renaissance, Realism & Early Indian English · Unit II: Poetry · Walt Whitman
items.stem: Who among the following is mourned in Walt Whitman's O Captain! My Captain!?
items.explanation: Whitman wrote this elegy on the death of Abraham Lincoln, the 'captain' of the ship of state.

items.title: Q86 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Sylvia Plath
items.stem:
Which artistic technique best describes the interplay of light and shade in the following lines?
"I have looked at it so long
I think it is part of my heart. But it flickers.
Faces and darkness separate us over and over
A woman bends over me,
Searching my reaches for what she really is
Then she turns to those liars, the candles or the moon.
I see her back, and reflect it faithfully."
items.explanation: Chiaroscuro is the contrast of light and dark. The flickering candle, the faces and the darkness create it in these lines (from Plath's 'Mirror').

items.title: Q87 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India
items.stem:
Which two titles from among the following deal with issues related to the institutionalisation of English in post-independence India?
(a) Provocations
(b) Professing Literature
(c) The Lie of the Land
(d) The Muse Unchained
The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: 'The Lie of the Land' (Sunder Rajan, ed.) and 'Provocations' deal with English studies in India. 'Professing Literature' and 'The Muse Unchained' concern the US and Britain.

items.title: Q88 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Philip Sidney
items.stem:
What, in sum, is Sidney's point in the following?
"Nature never set forth the earth in so rich tapestry as divers poets have done; neither with pleasant rivers, fruitful trees, sweet-smelling flowers, nor what so ever else may make the too-much-loved earth more lovely. Her world is brazen, the poets only deliver a golden." (Philip Sidney)
options: Works of art are superior to the natural world they represent
Works of art can often compete with the natural world represented by them
Neither the poets nor the natural world they set forth equal nature's rich tapestry
The natural world is far superior to the works of art that represent it
items.explanation: Sidney says nature's world is 'brazen' (base metal) while poets create a 'golden' one, so poetry improves on nature.

items.title: Q89 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
It is an axiom in mental philosophy, that we can think of nothing which we have not perceived. When I say that we can think of nothing, I mean we can imagine nothing, we can reason of nothing, we can remember nothing, we can foresee nothing. The most astonishing combinations of poetry, the subtlest deductions of logic and mathematics, are no other than combinations which the intellect makes of sensations according to its own laws. A catalogue of all the thoughts of the mind, and of all their possible modifications, is a cyclopaedic history of the universe.

According to the writer, perception is the basic epistemology. Which one of the following is the other accepted epistemology?
items.explanation: In Indian and other epistemology, the two accepted sources of knowledge are perception and inference.

items.title: Q90 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem:
It is an axiom in mental philosophy, that we can think of nothing which we have not perceived. When I say that we can think of nothing, I mean we can imagine nothing, we can reason of nothing, we can remember nothing, we can foresee nothing. The most astonishing combinations of poetry, the subtlest deductions of logic and mathematics, are no other than combinations which the intellect makes of sensations according to its own laws. A catalogue of all the thoughts of the mind, and of all their possible modifications, is a cyclopaedic history of the universe.

According to the passage given, which of the following correctly captures the meaning of 'a cyclopaedic history of the universe'?
options: The knowledge about the universe from its beginning to its possible end
A catalogue of rivers, mountains and continents
Statements about the universe based on logic and mathematics
A published encyclopaedia of the universe
items.explanation: If all thought comes from perception, a list of all thoughts would amount to complete knowledge of the universe.

items.title: Q91 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Miguel de Cervantes, Mark Twain, Thomas Mann
items.stem: Which one of the following words best describes the heroes of Cervantes' Don Quixote, Mark Twain's The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Thomas Mann's The Confessions of Felix Krull?
items.explanation: A picaro is a roguish, adventurous hero of episodic narratives. All three heroes fit this picaresque type.

items.title: Q92 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods · Edward Mendelson, Jerome McGann, Stanley Fish, Hugh Kenner
items.stem:
In the study of Anglo-American literatures, certain distinguished names in critical/editorial scholarship become synonymous with famous writers and periods of literary history.
Match the following names with their respective areas of scholarship :
(a) Edward Mendelson / (i) John Milton
(b) Jerome McGann / (ii) Ezra Pound
(c) Stanley Fish / (iii) W. H. Auden
(d) Hugh Kenner / (iv) Textual Scholarship
Choose the correct option from those given below :
items.explanation: Mendelson edited Auden, McGann is known for textual scholarship, Fish for Milton and Kenner for Pound.

items.title: Q93 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · John Updike
items.stem: Which of the following correctly list the two novels figuring the writer as a public figure, as a celebrity and as grist for the academic mill?
options: Rabbit is Rich and The Coup
Of the Farm and The Centaur
Bech: A Book and Bech is Back
items.explanation: John Updike's Henry Bech books, 'Bech: A Book' and 'Bech is Back', show a writer as a celebrity and academic subject.

items.title: Q94 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Elizabethan Period · Unit I: Drama · Thomas Nashe
items.stem: Who among the following is one of the University Wits?
items.explanation: The University Wits were Oxford and Cambridge educated writers like Marlowe, Greene, Lyly, Peele, Kyd and Nashe.

items.title: Q95 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII
items.stem:
Given below are two statements—one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R) :
Assertion (A) : Language constructs meaning.
Reason (R) : Language structures meanings depending on the speaking subjects' perception, context and auditor(s).
In the light of the above two statements choose the correct option :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)
items.explanation: Both are true. Meaning is built by language as it works through the speaker's view, context and listeners, so R explains A.

items.title: Q96 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Edwardian, Georgian & Irish Literary Revival · Unit I: Drama · George Bernard Shaw
items.stem:
Match the play with the subject matter of the play :
(a) The Doctor's Dilemma / (i) Flouting of stage conventions
(b) You Never Can Tell / (ii) Satire on military heroes
(c) Candida / (iii) Devaluation of social traditions
(d) Arms and the Man / (iv) Mockery of physicians' ignorance
Choose the correct option from those given below :
items.explanation: The Doctor's Dilemma mocks doctors, Arms and the Man satirises military heroes, You Never Can Tell devalues social traditions and Candida flouts stage conventions.

items.title: Q97 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
THE GROCER'S CHILDREN
The grocer's children
eat day-old bread,
moldy cakes and cheese,
soft black bananas
on stale shredded wheat,
weeviled rice, their plates
heaped high with wilted
greens, bruised fruit,
surprise treats
from unlabelled cans,
tainted meat.
The grocer's children
never go hungry.

Which of the following words best describes the last sentence of the poem?
items.explanation: The grocer's children eat spoiled food, so saying they 'never go hungry' is ironic: the words mean the opposite of the sad reality.

items.title: Q98 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
THE GROCER'S CHILDREN
The grocer's children
eat day-old bread,
moldy cakes and cheese,
soft black bananas
on stale shredded wheat,
weeviled rice, their plates
heaped high with wilted
greens, bruised fruit,
surprise treats
from unlabelled cans,
tainted meat.
The grocer's children
never go hungry.

What is suggested by the word 'tainted' in line 11?
items.explanation: 'Tainted' meat means meat that has gone bad or is contaminated, so spoiled.

items.title: Q99 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
THE GROCER'S CHILDREN
The grocer's children
eat day-old bread,
moldy cakes and cheese,
soft black bananas
on stale shredded wheat,
weeviled rice, their plates
heaped high with wilted
greens, bruised fruit,
surprise treats
from unlabelled cans,
tainted meat.
The grocer's children
never go hungry.

How does the poem achieve its effect?
options: It lists a number of grocery items which do not have any tangible nutritive benefit
It presents a series of inedible fare in the face of the basic need to eat
It strays away from the tongue-in-cheek beginning to state the obvious
It posits the circumspect existence of a reasonable plan to alleviate hunger
items.explanation: The poem piles up rotten, inedible foods against the basic need to eat, which gives it its bitter irony.

items.title: Q100 · June 2019 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit II: Poetry
items.stem:
THE GROCER'S CHILDREN
The grocer's children
eat day-old bread,
moldy cakes and cheese,
soft black bananas
on stale shredded wheat,
weeviled rice, their plates
heaped high with wilted
greens, bruised fruit,
surprise treats
from unlabelled cans,
tainted meat.
The grocer's children
never go hungry.

Whose point of view seems to have been stated in the poem?
items.explanation: The poem is told by an outside narrator who describes the children and comments on them, not by the grocer or the children.
